title: Parvati's grief
hookLine: Shiva meets the boy at his own door; Parvati's grief, the Goddess's power, stops the universe
tomorrow: Shiva has to bring the boy back. so where does he find a head?
last: THE HOLY CAN LIVE IN CLAY.

lines: A STRANGER AT HIS OWN DOOR.
cards: Here's a comment you might see under a video of a Ganesha festival: wait, his own dad cut his head off? Fair question, and the story has an answer. Why would a story like that be told at a festival full of kids?
Start where it starts. Shiva walks home up the mountain to his own house, and at his own door is a boy he has never seen. You can't come in, says the boy.
This is my house, says Shiva. My mother said no one. Shiva sends his ganas.
The boy beats them back. In the Shiva Purana, even the gods can't get past him. Then Shiva raises his trident.

teach.b: So, the puzzle. The story doesn't make anyone the villain. The boy is keeping his word to his mother.
Shiva is trying to walk into his own home. Both are right, and something terrible happens anyway. Then Parvati comes out.
In the Shiva Purana her grief is so big that she calls up fierce goddesses, forms of her own power, and sends them to swallow the universe.
Narada and the gods come pleading, and she names her terms: bring my son back, and honor him among you. And Shiva, the great god, does what she asks. Here's the teaching.
In Hinduism, God isn't only Father.

teach.h: SHAKTI: GOD AS MOTHER, GOD AS POWER.
teach.b: God is also Mother, and her name is Shakti: power, the energy that moves everything. Parvati is one face of her; Durga and Kali, with their weapons, are others. Many Hindus pray to her simply as Ma.
A saying many know plays on the letters: take the i of Shakti out of Shiva, and you get shava, a corpse. The god and his power can't be pulled apart.

Nobody tells this mother to calm down. Her grief is the power of the universe, and even Shiva answers it. That's why a story like this can be told at a festival full of kids: it's a mother's love, bringing her child home.

how: Many Hindus worship God as the Mother, Shakti, in forms like Parvati, Durga and Kali, and call on her simply as Ma. This story is told as part of Ganesha's birth, often at Ganesh Chaturthi.

o: a lamp Parvati lit to welcome Shiva home
a ceremonial bell rung at a temple's door
Shiva's three-pointed spear, raised at his door

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: keeps his word: no one comes in
God as Mother, the power in everything

s: in the story, one of them is clearly the villain
both are right: the boy keeps his word, Shiva tries to enter his own home.
Parvati's grief threatens the whole universe
in the Shiva Purana she sends fierce goddesses to swallow the worlds until her son is restored.
in Hinduism, God is only ever pictured as a father
God is also worshipped as Mother: Shakti, the power that moves everything. Parvati, Durga and Kali are her faces.

games.q: your little cousin asks: why did Shiva, the great god, do what Parvati said? what fits today's teaching?
o: because Parvati is Shakti, the Goddess's power. even Shiva answers her.
because he was scared of getting in trouble.
because in stories the gods always take the easy way out.
games.why: in Hinduism God is also Mother. Parvati's grief is Shakti, the power that moves everything, and Shiva and the gods answer it.

practice: For two minutes, bring to mind the strongest woman you know, the one whose care held your world together: a mother, a grandmother, an aunt, a teacher.
Many Hindus pray to the Goddess with one word, Ma, said softly on the out-breath; if you pray, try it. If you don't, say her name instead, with a quiet thank you.

wordCard.voice: Trident: Shiva's three-pointed spear, trishula in Sanskrit, three spears. Raised at a door, it set off a grief even Shiva had to answer.

orig.note: Sanskrit: three spears, the trident Shiva carries.

carryVoice: Hold onto this one: God is also Mother, and her name is Shakti. Even Shiva answers her. Day twenty-three, done.
